title: Design a Distributed Lock / Coordination Service
prompt: Design a distributed locking / coordination service that lets processes across many machines acquire mutual-exclusion locks (and elect leaders) safely. Cover how a lock is acquired and released, what happens when the holder crashes or is partitioned, and how you prevent two processes from ever believing they hold the same lock.
blurb: The mutual-exclusion-across-machines problem — leases with expiry, fencing tokens against stale holders, and the Redlock-vs-consensus safety debate.

rubric.label: Requirements gathering
rubric.description: Separates functional (acquire/release, TTL, leader election, wait/notify) from non-functional (correctness/safety, liveness, availability, low latency).

rubric.label: Clarifying questions
rubric.description: Asks whether the lock guards correctness or is just an optimization, lock hold time, contention level, acceptable failure modes, latency tolerance.

rubric.label: Safety vs liveness framing
rubric.description: Recognizes the core tension: you cannot have a lock that is always both safe (never two holders) and live (always grantable) under partitions; picks a stance and justifies it.

rubric.label: Leases & expiry
rubric.description: Locks as time-bounded leases (not held forever), renewal/heartbeat, why unbounded locks deadlock on crash, and clock-dependence risks.

rubric.label: Fencing tokens
rubric.description: Monotonic fencing tokens so a paused/stale holder's writes are rejected by the resource; why TTL alone is insufficient (GC pause / clock skew).

rubric.label: Consensus / backing store
rubric.description: Backing the lock on a consensus system (Raft/Paxos, ZooKeeper/etcd) for a single source of truth; ephemeral nodes/sessions; vs a single Redis or Redlock.

rubric.label: High-level design
rubric.description: Client -> lock service (consensus-backed) issuing leases + monotonic tokens; session/heartbeat; leader election via the same primitive.

rubric.label: Failure handling
rubric.description: Holder crash (auto-release on lease expiry), network partition (holder can't renew), clock skew, split-brain avoidance.

rubric.label: Redlock & alternatives tradeoffs
rubric.description: Understands the Redlock debate (majority of independent Redis nodes) vs a single consensus system; where each is safe/unsafe and why fencing still matters.

rubric.label: Bottlenecks
rubric.description: Consensus write throughput, lock-service availability as a dependency, herd on a hot lock, heartbeat load.

rubric.label: Observability
rubric.description: Lock acquire/hold/wait times, expired-lease reclaims, contention/queue depth, leader-election churn, token gaps.

functional_requirements: Acquire and release a named lock (mutual exclusion)
Locks are leases with a TTL and can be renewed
Leader election (a single holder among contenders)
Wait/queue for a lock and get notified on availability
Return a fencing token with each grant
nonfunctional_requirements: Safety: never two live holders of the same lock (for correctness locks)
Liveness: a crashed holder's lock is eventually reclaimable
High availability of the lock service itself
Low acquire latency under normal conditions
Correct behavior under partitions, GC pauses, and clock skew
clarifying_questions: Is the lock protecting correctness (must never double-hold) or just an efficiency optimization (occasional double-hold is tolerable)?
Typical lock hold time and contention level?
How is the protected resource accessed — can it check a fencing token?
What latency is acceptable to acquire a lock?
Do we also need leader election and change notifications?
qualifying_questions: Under a partition, do you prefer to block (safe) or grant anyway (available)?
Are clocks trustworthy, or must we assume unbounded GC pauses/skew?
How many locks and acquire rate — is this a hot coordination primitive?

estimations.throughput: Every acquire/release/renew is a write through consensus; a Raft group tops out at low tens of thousands of ops/s — shard locks across groups if you need more.
estimations.heartbeat: N holders renewing every T seconds = N/T renew ops/s baseline load; short TTLs mean faster reclaim but more heartbeat traffic.
estimations.latency: Consensus commit adds a round-trip (single-digit ms intra-region); cross-region raises it and the availability question.
estimations.sharding: Partition the lock namespace across multiple consensus groups to scale write throughput.

core_components: Lock service backed by consensus (Raft/Paxos; e.g. etcd/ZooKeeper-like)
api_design: acquire(lock_id, ttl) -> { granted, fencing_token, lease_expiry } | queued
release(lock_id, session) -> frees lock, notifies next waiter
watch(lock_id) -> notification when the lock frees / leader changes
reference.high_level_design: Locks live in a strongly-consistent, consensus-backed store (a Raft/Paxos group, ZooKeeper/etcd-style). A client acquires a lock as a lease with a TTL; the grant includes a monotonically increasing fencing token. The client must renew (heartbeat) before expiry or the lease auto-expires and the lock becomes reclaimable — so a crashed or partitioned holder can't hold forever. Because a holder can be paused (GC) or partitioned and not realize its lease expired, TTL alone is unsafe: the protected resource must require the fencing token and reject any write carrying a token lower than the highest it has seen. Leader election is the same primitive (whoever holds the 'leader' lock leads). Waiters watch the lock and are notified/queued for fairness. Everything routes through consensus so there is one authoritative view of who holds what.

deep_dives.probe: Client A acquires the lock, then GC-pauses for 20s; its lease expires and B acquires. A wakes and writes to the resource believing it still holds the lock. TTL didn't save you. How do fencing tokens make A's write safe to reject?

Under a network partition you can keep the lock safe (refuse to grant) or available (grant anyway). You can't have both. Which do you choose for a correctness lock, and why does that map to CP over AP?
Why leases with TTL rather than hold-until-release? How do you pick the TTL vs heartbeat interval, and what breaks if clocks drift between client and server?
Walk through Redlock (acquire on a majority of independent Redis nodes). Where is it unsafe, and why does Kleppmann's critique say you still need fencing tokens regardless of the locking algorithm?
Why back this on Raft/Paxos (etcd/ZooKeeper) instead of a single Redis? What do ephemeral nodes/sessions give you for automatic release on client death?

Lock state (holders, grants, token issuance) lives in the consensus store. How would you stream lock events out to an audit log, metrics, or a dashboard — change data capture / watching the store's change stream — without dual-writing and risking a divergent audit view?

followup_bank.question: Where is Redlock unsafe (clock skew, GC pause, lost node state), and why do you still need fencing tokens even if the lock algorithm were perfect?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions ttl or lease or expiry
followup_bank.question: A holder GC-pauses past its TTL and another client acquires — how do you prevent the stale holder's write from corrupting the resource? (fencing)
If lock state sits in an in-memory store, what's the eviction/expiry semantics on a node restart, and how do you avoid a herd when a hot lock frees and all waiters retry at once?

followup_bank.trigger: mentions zookeeper or etcd or raft or consensus or database
followup_bank.question: How do you stream lock/leader-election state changes to audit and monitoring — CDC / the store's watch stream vs dual writes — without a divergent audit trail?
During a partition, do you favor safety (block) or liveness (grant)? Map that decision to CP vs AP.

scaling: Shard the lock namespace across multiple consensus groups for write throughput
Use short TTLs + heartbeats to reclaim fast; longer TTLs to cut heartbeat load
Client-side backoff/jitter on contended locks to avoid herds
Read-only lock status from followers where staleness is acceptable
Batch/co-locate related locks in the same group to reduce cross-group coordination
bottlenecks: Consensus write throughput (every op is a committed write)
The lock service as a hard dependency / availability floor
Herd on a hot lock when it frees
tradeoffs: Consensus-backed (safe, single source of truth, lower throughput) vs Redis/Redlock (fast, weaker safety)
Short TTL (fast reclaim, more heartbeats) vs long TTL (less traffic, slow reclaim)
Safety-first under partition (CP, may block) vs availability-first (AP, may double-grant)
Fencing tokens (safe but resource must cooperate) vs trusting TTL alone (simpler, unsafe)
alternative_solutions: ZooKeeper ephemeral sequential znodes for locks + leader election
Single Redis with SET NX PX (optimization locks only)
Redlock across independent Redis nodes (contested safety)
Database row lock / advisory lock (simple, limited scale)
observability: Contention and waiter-queue depth per lock
Fencing-token issuance and any out-of-order token rejections
security: Authn/authz on who may acquire which locks
Prevent forged fencing tokens (issued only by the service, verified by the resource)
Rate-limit acquire attempts to prevent abuse/DoS on hot locks
Audit trail of grants and leader changes
reference.reference_answer: A strong answer first asks whether the lock guards correctness or is an optimization, because that sets the safety bar. It models locks as leases with TTL + heartbeat (so crashed holders auto-release) and backs them on a consensus system (Raft/Paxos, ZooKeeper/etcd) for a single authoritative view, with ephemeral sessions for auto-release on client death. Crucially it explains why TTL alone is unsafe under GC pauses/clock skew and requires monotonic fencing tokens that the protected resource enforces. It articulates the safety-vs-liveness (CP vs AP) tradeoff under partitions and takes a stance, critiques Redlock (unsafe timing assumptions; fencing needed regardless), shards locks across consensus groups for throughput, and streams lock state to audit via CDC/watch rather than dual writes.

interviewer_notes: This question separates engineers who've operated distributed systems from those who haven't. The two must-hit insights are fencing tokens (TTL alone cannot prevent a GC-paused holder from writing after its lease expired) and the safety-vs-liveness/CP-vs-AP tradeoff under partitions — drive the GC-pause scenario explicitly and see if they reach for a monotonic token. Expect them to prefer a consensus-backed store over a single Redis and to engage with the Redlock debate honestly. If they mention Redis/cache, probe expiry semantics and herd on lock release; if they mention ZooKeeper/etcd/a datastore, hit the CDC/watch-stream audit probe. Reward asking whether the lock protects correctness up front.
